studies.label: Phase 2: randomized constructive-comment writing experiment

counts_source.locator: PDF p. 2 (printed p. 410:2), Introduction, Phase 2 description; corroborated by Table 5 on PDF p. 12 (printed p. 410:12)
counts_source.quote: In Phase 2, to examine how LLMs facilitate constructive writing, we conducted a between- subject experiment with a different set of 103 Indian and American crowd workers on Prolific.

arms.name: HAI-written comments (test)
arms.description: Participants drafted their own comments, requested GPT-4 rewriting using listed or custom prompts, and could accept, reject, regenerate, or edit suggestions before submitting; a model request was required (PDF pp. 10-11, Section 3.2).

arms.name: Human-written comments (control)
arms.description: Participants wrote constructive comments independently without external assistance, including the Internet or ChatGPT (PDF p. 10, Section 3.2).

studies.task: Write a constructive comment expressing one’s own stance on each of a homophobic and an Islamophobic thread relevant to one’s country.

ai_tool.name: GPT-4; exact snapshot not stated
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 410:10), Section 3.2, Writing Task; rewriting interface and prompt on PDF p. 11 (printed p. 410:11); release year is not stated

estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Semantic similarity among comments by different writers on the same thread with the same stance (Section 4.2.3, PDF pp. 17-18). Methods name the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence transformer for draft-final semantic similarity (PDF p. 12); the cross-writer section does not independently restate its implementation.

sources.locator: PDF p. 18 (printed p. 410:18), Table 8, Semantic similarity row; control then test columns

estimates.notes: The paper compares different writers in the same arm who responded to the same thread and shared the same stance. It does not specify pair enumeration, aggregation, or the statistical observation unit. Analysis-specific numbers of writers and participant-level uncertainty are not printed. No arm people count is inferred from comment counts. Table 8 prints a dash in the statistics column and the prose reports no significant difference. No numeric U, Z, p-value, effect size, SD, SE, or confidence interval is supplied; no p-value is inferred from the dash.

estimates.outcome: Human-rated constructiveness: preference for a comment in a forced-choice pair
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Independent Prolific evaluators selected the more constructive comment in a same-thread, same-stance pair. Arm levels are percentages of pair evaluations preferring that arm, not a continuous creativity rating (PDF pp. 12, 14-15).

sources.locator: PDF p. 15 (printed p. 410:15), Section 4.2.1, Human Evaluation of Constructiveness; test also in Table 6, HAI vs. Human, Both demographic
sources.quote: significantly more constructive than human-written comments in 64% of cases, with small effect size (𝜒2(1, 𝑁= 802) = 62.56, 𝑝< 0.000005,𝜙= 0.28, odds ratio=3.19).

sources.locator: PDF p. 14 (printed p. 410:14), Section 4.2.1, Human Evaluation of Constructiveness
sources.quote: which included 401 pairs of HAI vs. Human comments

estimates.notes: The outcome evaluates quality of the randomized writers’ comments; it is retained as usefulness, not a separate perception experiment or an independent writer sample. Higher preference means greater rated constructiveness. The treatment level remains in the printed percentage units. The human-only percentage appears only as a label in Figure 4, so control_mean is null under the no-figure-only-number rule. The additional phi coefficient and the chi-square N are preserved in the source quote; the latter is not a writer count. n_units counts evaluated pairs, not necessarily distinct pairs. The paper does not explain the contingency-table construction or reconcile its chi-square N with the evaluated-pair total, so the uncertainty basis is unclear. No writer-clustered or participant-level uncertainty is reported. The number of distinct writers contributing to this particular contrast is not printed.

estimates.outcome: Cosine similarity of word-count vectors across writers
estimates.question: across_people
estimates.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of comments by different writers on the same thread with the same stance (Section 4.2.3, PDF pp. 17-18). Methods name scikit-learn CountVectorizer for draft-final cosine similarity (PDF p. 12); the cross-writer section does not independently restate its implementation. This is lexical similarity, not an embedding-based creativity score.

open_items: Randomized people counts and arm-specific analyzed people counts are not printed. Recruitment and completion counts differ without an explained participant flow (PDF p. 12). No people count is derived from the number of comments.
The study-level analyzed writer total is printed, but analysis-specific distinct-writer totals are not. Estimate n_treatment, n_control, and n_total therefore remain null.

For cross-writer similarity, pair enumeration, aggregation, the independent observation unit, number of observations, and participant-level dependence handling are unspecified (PDF pp. 17-19, Table 8).

Distinct-2 and TTR may describe vocabulary within comments or a pooled corpus. Their cross-person diversity interpretation cannot be confirmed; other/with_ai and null unit are retained pending the analysis code (PDF pp. 18-19).

Human-evaluation pair totals, the stated allocation procedure, and chi-square N values are not reconciled. The contingency table, odds-ratio construction, and writer-level precision are not provided (PDF pp. 12, 14-15).

Full-sample arm means for linguistic features are not numerically printed outside the plots. Country-specific means are not substitutes. Participant-level SDs, SEs, and confidence intervals are absent (Figure 5; Tables 15 and 19).
The standardizer for the reported rank-test effect r is not stated; no conversion to a standardized mean difference is attempted (Tables 8 and 15).

The paper interprets higher SMOG scores as better readability, but the measure is a readability index rather than a direct creativity score. The extraction preserves the raw test and flags its direction as other (PDF pp. 9 and 16).
No model snapshot or release year is printed for the GPT-4 assistance tool; ai_tool.year remains null (PDF pp. 10-11).
The saved arXiv v5 and the later journal version have not been compared; this extraction applies only to the local PDF.
notes: The complete markdown conversion was read, including references and Appendix A, after the PDF tables and figures were inventoried. All numeric fields and their source quotations were checked against PyMuPDF page text or recovered table cells. Only the randomized writing experiment is retained in studies; its reconciled screening identifier S4 and exact arm names are preserved. Other experimental phases are listed in not_extracted. No external-paper sample overlap is reported. Within-paper evaluators are distinct from writers; their judgments of S4 outputs do not create a separate writer sample. The current codebook’s length and text_features measure codes are used where applicable, updating the older screening form’s null codes. Full-sample contrasts remain as records even when their only arm values are unlabeled graphical means. Auxiliary Z statistics and the phi coefficient are retained verbatim in source quotes because the template has one test object and one paper_effect object per contrast. Reported U and r signs and printed decimal precision are preserved in those quotes. No statistical value, people count, arm average, or figure value was computed. Numeric source locators identify physical PDF pages and the printed article-page labels.
